concepts.title: The kubectl Debugging Workflow: describe, logs, exec
concepts.description: kubectl get, describe, logs, and exec each answer a different question about a broken Pod. Knowing which one to reach for first, and the trap each one has (a stale --previous log, a container that isn't Running yet), turns 'my Pod is broken' from a guessing game into a short, repeatable diagnostic sequence.
learningObjectives: Use kubectl get pods to identify which lifecycle stage a broken Pod is stuck in from its STATUS and RESTARTS columns.
Use kubectl describe pod to read the Events section and map specific event reasons to the component and stage responsible.
Use kubectl logs, including --previous and -c, to read a crashed container's own output rather than a fresh restart's near-empty log stream.
Use kubectl exec to inspect a live, Running container's environment, mounted files, and connectivity to a dependency.
Explain why kubectl exec and kubectl logs --previous target fundamentally different moments in a container's lifecycle, and why picking the wrong one wastes time.
Use kubectl port-forward to reach a specific Pod directly, bypassing its Service, to isolate whether a problem is in the Pod or in the networking layer in front of it.

sections.heading: Start With kubectl get pods: The STATUS Column Is a Map
sections.body:
Before reaching for deeper tools, `kubectl get pods` gives a fast, cheap read on which *stage* of a Pod's lifecycle is broken, and that decides which tool is worth trying next. `Pending` means the Pod hasn't been scheduled yet; nothing has started running, so `kubectl logs` and `kubectl exec` have nothing to show you. (A Pod waiting on init containers shows `Init:0/1` and similar instead.) `ContainerCreating` means it's been scheduled and the kubelet is working on it, commonly pulling an image. `ImagePullBackOff`/`ErrImagePull` means the image pull is failing (wrong tag, private registry auth, network). `CrashLoopBackOff` means the container starts, then exits, repeatedly, with the kubelet waiting increasingly long between restart attempts. `Running` means the container process is alive, which says nothing about whether the *application* inside is healthy or serving requests correctly.

The `RESTARTS` column is worth reading alongside `STATUS`: a Pod showing `Running` with `RESTARTS: 14` and climbing isn't healthy. It keeps crashing and getting restarted by the kubelet, and is caught mid-cycle between one crash and the next, broken in the same way as one currently showing `CrashLoopBackOff`. Treating `Running` as automatically meaning 'fine' is one of the most common ways people waste time investigating the wrong thing first. To see why the last instance died without opening `describe`, read it from the Pod's status: `kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState}'` shows the previous instance's exit code and reason.

sections.heading: kubectl describe pod: Reading the Events Section
sections.body:
`kubectl describe pod <name>` prints the Pod's full spec and status, but the most useful part for debugging is at the bottom: a chronological **Events** table, the same event stream introduced in the Cluster Architecture concept, filtered to this one object.

```text
Events:
  Type     Reason     Age   From               Message
  ----     ------     ----  ----               -------
  Normal   Scheduled  2m    default-scheduler  Successfully assigned default/web-abc to node-2
  Normal   Pulling    2m    kubelet            Pulling image "my-app:1.4"
  Normal   Pulled     1m    kubelet            Successfully pulled image "my-app:1.4"
  Normal   Created    1m    kubelet            Created container app
  Normal   Started    1m    kubelet            Started container app
  Warning  Unhealthy  30s   kubelet            Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 500
  Normal   Killing    30s   kubelet            Container app failed liveness probe, will be restarted
  Warning  BackOff    10s   kubelet            Back-off restarting failed container
```

Each `Reason` maps onto a component and stage you already know: `Scheduled` is the scheduler's output; `Pulling`/`Pulled`/`Created`/`Started` are the kubelet driving the container runtime through startup; `FailedScheduling` (not shown above) means the scheduler couldn't place the Pod at all, with a message like `0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu`. Reading the table top to bottom tells you which stage the Pod got stuck at, which is why `describe`, not `logs`, should usually be the *second* command you run (right after `get pods`): it tells you whether the problem is even inside the container's code yet, or happened before the container had a chance to run. When the Pod has already been deleted or you want the whole namespace's recent history, `kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp` shows the same stream across all objects, newest last.

sections.heading: kubectl logs and the --previous Trap
sections.body:
`kubectl logs <pod>` streams the stdout/stderr of the Pod's (single) container's *current* process. For a Pod in `CrashLoopBackOff` this is where people waste the most time: the *currently running* instance is often a fresh restart that has barely started and hasn't reached the code path that crashes, so `kubectl logs` shows little or nothing, and it's tempting to conclude 'there's nothing in the logs' when the crash's output is one restart back.

`kubectl logs <pod> --previous` (or `-p`) is the fix: it retrieves the logs of the *immediately preceding, already-terminated* container instance, the one that crashed, instead of the current one that may not have failed yet. This one flag resolves most 'the logs are empty but the Pod is clearly crashing' confusion. Two more flags help on busy Pods: `--since=10m` limits output to recent lines, and `--timestamps` prefixes each line with its time, which makes it easy to line the log up against the Events table.

```bash
kubectl logs web-abc123                 # current instance (may be nearly empty right after a fresh restart)
kubectl logs web-abc123 --previous      # the instance that actually crashed
kubectl logs web-abc123 -c sidecar      # multi-container Pod: name the container; the default is only the first
kubectl logs web-abc123 -f --tail=50    # follow new output live, starting from the last 50 lines
```

On a Pod with more than one container, `kubectl logs` without `-c` shows only the default container (the first one, unless the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container` annotation says otherwise) and prints a 'Defaulted container ... out of: ...' note to stderr, so a failing sidecar's logs are easy to miss. Name the container with `-c <container-name>`, or use `--all-containers` to read them all. (Older kubectl versions instead refused with 'a container name must be specified'.) A Pod's containers have independent log streams; nothing merges them.

sections.heading: kubectl exec, Ephemeral Debug Containers, and port-forward
sections.body:
`kubectl exec -it <pod> -- /bin/sh` opens an interactive shell *inside* a currently **Running** container, letting you check things no external tool can see: resolved environment variables (`env`), whether a ConfigMap/Secret volume mount contains what you expect (`cat /etc/app-config/LOG_LEVEL`), whether the container can reach a dependency (`curl -v http://db:5432`, `nslookup db`), or what processes are running (`ps aux`).

This only works on a container that is `Running` right now. It can't attach to a Pod stuck `Pending`, `ContainerCreating`, or mid-crash in `CrashLoopBackOff` between restarts, because there's no live process to attach to. A second limitation: many production images (especially minimal 'distroless' base images, built without a shell or package manager to shrink attack surface) have no `/bin/sh`, so `kubectl exec` fails with 'executable file not found,' not because the container is unhealthy but because there's no shell binary to run. `kubectl debug <pod> -it --image=busybox --target=<container>` sidesteps this by attaching a *separate*, throwaway 'ephemeral container' with a real shell to the same Pod, sharing its network and (with `--target`) process namespace, without modifying or restarting the original container.

`kubectl port-forward pod/<name> 8080:80` opens a tunnel from your local machine to one specific Pod, bypassing any Service, Endpoints, or kube-proxy in front of it. It answers a narrow question: 'is the problem inside this Pod, or in the Service/networking layer in front of it?' If `curl localhost:8080` works after a port-forward but the Service still fails, the bug lives in the selector/Endpoints/kube-proxy layer covered in the Services concept, not in the Pod.

sections.heading: Putting It Together: A Systematic Diagnosis Order
sections.body:
A workable default sequence for 'this Pod is broken and I don't yet know why': (1) `kubectl get pods`: read STATUS and RESTARTS to see which stage is broken. (2) `kubectl describe pod`: read the Events in the order shown to see where the sequence stalled or what failed. (3) If the container has started at least once, `kubectl logs --previous` (and plain `kubectl logs` if it's Running and you want live behavior) to see what the application said. (4) If the container is Running and the mystery remains, `kubectl exec` in to inspect live state.

Common mistakes, each of which wastes time: jumping to `kubectl logs` before `describe`, and so missing a `FailedScheduling` or `ImagePullBackOff` event that explains everything before the container ran any application code; forgetting `--previous` on a crash-looping Pod and concluding 'the logs are empty' when they're the wrong instance's logs; forgetting `-c <container>` on a multi-container Pod and reading the wrong container's logs; and trying `kubectl exec` on a Pod that `kubectl get pods` already showed as `Pending` or `CrashLoopBackOff` between restarts, when no live process exists to attach to.

examples.title: From get to describe: Locating a Scheduling Failure
examples.code:
kubectl get pods
# NAME        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# web-abc123  0/1     Pending   0          6m

kubectl describe pod web-abc123 | tail -6
# Events:
#   Type     Reason            Age   From               Message
#   ----     ------            ----  ----               -------
#   Warning  FailedScheduling  6m    default-scheduler  0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory.
examples.explanation: STATUS: Pending with 0 RESTARTS and 6 minutes of age is the first strong signal that this Pod never got past scheduling. There's no point running kubectl logs or kubectl exec, since no container has started. describe pod's Events table confirms why: FailedScheduling, from the scheduler, with a message naming the constraint (Insufficient memory) that no node could satisfy. This is the same class of failure as the Cluster Architecture concept's exercise: the fix lives in the Pod's resources.requests or the cluster's node capacity, not in anything log- or exec-related, because the container has never run.

examples.title: The --previous Flag Revealing an Otherwise-Invisible Crash
examples.code:
kubectl get pods
# NAME        READY   STATUS             RESTARTS   AGE
# web-abc123  0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   5          3m

kubectl logs web-abc123
# (empty: the current instance restarted seconds ago and hasn't reached the crash point yet)

kubectl logs web-abc123 --previous
# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   File "app.py", line 12, in <module>
#     db = connect(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"])
# KeyError: 'DATABASE_URL'
examples.explanation: The plain kubectl logs call looks like a dead end, with no output, which is the trap this concept warns about: the current container instance is a fresh restart that hasn't run long enough to hit the crashing code path again. Adding --previous retrieves the logs from the instance one restart back, the one that crashed, and reveals the cause: the application reads os.environ["DATABASE_URL"] and finds it unset, a KeyError that kills the process on every startup. That points at a missing environment variable, most likely an envFrom/configMapKeyRef reference left out of the Deployment's Pod template, tying back to the ConfigMaps and Secrets concept.

examples.title: kubectl exec to Verify a Mounted Secret, and kubectl debug for a Shell-less Image
examples.code:
kubectl exec -it web-abc123 -- sh -c 'ls /etc/secrets && cat /etc/secrets/password | wc -c'
# password
# 0
# (the file exists but is empty: the Secret's value is probably empty, since a missing or misnamed key would leave no file at all; not a mount-path problem)

# Against a distroless image with no shell at all:
kubectl exec -it web-abc123 -- sh
# OCI runtime exec failed: exec failed: unable to start container process: exec: "sh": executable file not found in $PATH

kubectl debug -it web-abc123 --image=busybox --target=app
# (attaches a separate, throwaway container with a real shell into the same Pod,
#  sharing its network namespace, letting you curl localhost or inspect /proc/<pid>/root)
examples.explanation: The first command uses exec to answer a question no external tool can: is the Secret volume mounted, and does the file inside it have content? An empty file (0 bytes) rules out 'the volume isn't mounted' and points at the Secret's value being empty (a key that didn't exist would leave no file at all). The second and third commands show the shell-less-image failure and its fix: a distroless or minimal image has no sh binary for exec to run, so the answer isn't to retry exec but to attach an ephemeral debug container with kubectl debug, which brings its own shell without touching the original container's image.

misconceptions.description: kubectl logs <pod> always shows whatever caused the container's most recent crash, since that's clearly the most relevant thing that happened to it recently.
misconceptions.clarification: kubectl logs with no flags shows the CURRENT container instance's output. For a Pod that's crash-looping, the current instance is often a fresh restart that hasn't run long enough to reach the code path that crashes, so its log can be empty or unhelpful even though the Pod is failing repeatedly. The crash's output belongs to the PREVIOUS, already-terminated instance, retrievable with kubectl logs --previous. Treating a lack of output from the plain command as 'nothing to see here' is one of the most common time-wasting mistakes in Kubernetes debugging.

misconceptions.description: kubectl exec will work on any Pod that shows up in kubectl get pods, since the Pod obviously exists.
misconceptions.clarification: kubectl exec needs a container that is currently in the Running state with a live process to attach to. It fails against a Pod stuck Pending or ContainerCreating (nothing has started) and against a Pod caught between restart attempts in CrashLoopBackOff (the previous process has exited and the next hasn't started). It can also fail against a Pod that IS Running if the container's image has no shell binary (common in minimal/distroless images), in which case the fix is kubectl debug with an ephemeral debug container, not retrying exec against the original container.

exercises.prompt: A Pod shows `STATUS: CrashLoopBackOff` and `RESTARTS: 8`. `kubectl describe pod` shows Events ending in `Liveness probe failed` followed by `Killing` and `BackOff`. `kubectl logs <pod>` shows nothing useful. What single next command is most likely to reveal the actual application-level error, and why would plain `kubectl logs` (without that addition) keep failing to show it?
exercises.code:
kubectl get pods
# web-abc123   0/1   CrashLoopBackOff   8   4m

kubectl logs web-abc123
# (empty or unhelpful)
hints: The container currently running is very likely a fresh restart -- how much time has it had to reach whatever code path is actually failing?
There's a specific flag for retrieving the logs of the container instance that existed immediately before the current one.
The failing instance's own output is not gone -- it's just not the one kubectl logs shows you by default.
exercises.expectedAnswer: kubectl logs web-abc123 --previous. The currently running instance is a fresh restart that likely hasn't yet reached the point where it fails again, so its own logs are sparse or empty; --previous retrieves the logs of the immediately preceding, already-terminated instance, the one that crashed, which is where the real error message will be.
exercises.solutionExplanation: With RESTARTS climbing and the events showing repeated liveness-probe kills, this container is in a crash loop, and the kubelet's back-off delay means the current instance may be too young to have reached the failure again. kubectl logs targets only the current instance by default, which is why it's empty: the crash output belongs to the previous instance. kubectl logs web-abc123 --previous retrieves that terminated instance's stdout/stderr, where whatever caused the original liveness failure (an unhandled exception, a fatal startup error, a slowdown) would be visible.

exercises.prompt: A script used during incidents runs `kubectl logs app-pod-xyz` to capture the output of the `log-shipper` sidecar, but it always prints the `app` container's logs instead, with a 'Defaulted container "app" out of: app, log-shipper' note on stderr. It works as intended against simpler single-container Pods. Find and fix the bug.
hints: This behavior only appears against Pods with more than one container -- what does the app-pod-xyz Pod's spec likely contain that a simpler Pod's doesn't?
With more than one container in the Pod, kubectl logs reads a default container (the first) unless you name one, and it never merges the containers' output.
The fix is adding a flag that names exactly one container to read logs from.
exercises.solutionCode:
kubectl get pod app-pod-xyz -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}'
# app  log-shipper

kubectl logs app-pod-xyz -c log-shipper
exercises.solutionExplanation: The target Pod has multiple containers (a main app container plus a log-shipper sidecar). Without -c, kubectl logs reads the Pod's default container, the first one, and notes that on stderr, so the script captured the wrong stream; older kubectl versions instead refused with 'a container name must be specified.' The fix is to list the Pod's container names (via kubectl get pod ... -o jsonpath, or kubectl describe pod) and pass -c <container-name> to read the one you mean. This is the multi-container detail from the Pods concept: a Pod's containers are independent processes with independent log streams, and sharing a Pod doesn't merge them.

assessments.prompt: A Pod shows `STATUS: Pending` with `RESTARTS: 0` and has been in that state for 10 minutes. What is the most appropriate next debugging command, and why?
options: kubectl describe pod <pod>, to read the Events section and see why the Pod hasn't been scheduled or started yet.
kubectl port-forward pod/<pod> 8080:80, to test connectivity directly against the Pod, and confirm the application is listening.
kubectl logs <pod> --previous, to see what caused the most recent crash.
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh, to inspect the container's environment directly.
assessments.explanation: Pending with zero restarts means no container in this Pod has started: there's no live process to exec into (ruling out the “kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh…” option), no previous crashed instance to take logs from (ruling out the “kubectl logs <pod> --previous, to see what…” option), and nothing listening on a port to forward traffic to (ruling out the “kubectl port-forward pod/<pod> 8080:80, to test connectivity…” option). kubectl describe pod's Events section is the tool for this stage, since it surfaces either a scheduling failure (FailedScheduling, naming the resource or constraint) or shows an init container still running or stuck, either way revealing why the Pod hasn't progressed past Pending.

assessments.prompt: A Pod shows `STATUS: Running` with `RESTARTS: 14`, and the number keeps climbing. What does this actually indicate?
options: Running with any nonzero RESTARTS count always means a human operator manually restarted the container via kubectl, never the kubelet acting automatically.
The Pod is functionally in the same broken category as one showing CrashLoopBackOff -- it's currently caught mid-cycle between one crash and the next.
RESTARTS only increments when a Pod is deleted and replaced by its own controller, so a high, climbing count here actually indicates a ReplicaSet functioning correctly.
The Pod is healthy -- Running is the only status that matters, and RESTARTS is purely a historical counter with no bearing on current health.
assessments.explanation: A Pod showing Running with RESTARTS: 14 and climbing is not healthy: it keeps crashing and being restarted by the kubelet, and is caught mid-cycle. This is one of the most common ways people waste time investigating the wrong thing first. The “The Pod is healthy -- Running…” option falls into that trap. The “RESTARTS only increments when a Pod…” option misattributes RESTARTS to Pod replacement by a controller, when it counts container restarts within the same Pod object. The “Running with any nonzero RESTARTS count always…” option is false: nearly all restarts are the kubelet acting automatically per restartPolicy, not manual operator action.

assessments.prompt: `kubectl exec -it` into a Running container fails with 'executable file not found in $PATH' when trying to run `sh`. What does this specific error most likely indicate, and what's the appropriate next step?
options: The Pod hasn't actually reached the Running state yet, despite what kubectl get pods reports, and exec is failing for the same underlying reason it would against a Pending Pod.
This error specifically means the container has no readiness probe configured, and one must be added before exec will succeed.

The container's image is likely a minimal/distroless image built without a shell binary at all -- exec has nothing to run inside the container regardless of its health; the appropriate fix is kubectl debug with an ephemeral container that brings its own shell along.
The container is unhealthy and about to crash; the fix is to wait and retry exec once it stabilizes.
assessments.explanation: Many production images have no /bin/sh, so kubectl exec into them fails with 'executable file not found,' not because the container is unhealthy but because there's no shell binary to run. The fix is kubectl debug with an ephemeral container, which attaches its own shell without modifying the original image. The “The container is unhealthy and about…” option misdiagnoses a missing binary as a health problem. The “The Pod hasn't actually reached the Running…” option contradicts the premise: the scenario says the container is Running. The “This error specifically means the container has…” option invents a dependency between readiness probes and exec.

assessments.prompt: `kubectl port-forward pod/web-abc123 8080:80` is used, and curling `localhost:8080` locally works perfectly. However, requests routed through the Pod's Service still fail. What does this specifically isolate the problem to?
options: The problem must be inside the Pod's own application code, since port-forward and the Service ultimately reach the same container either way.
The problem must be a liveness probe misconfiguration, since only a liveness failure could cause a Service to fail while direct Pod access still succeeds.
The comparison is meaningless, since port-forward and Services always use fundamentally different, incompatible port numbering schemes.
The problem lies in the Service/Endpoints/kube-proxy layer sitting in front of the Pod, not in the Pod itself.
assessments.explanation: port-forward answers the question 'is the problem inside this Pod, or in the Service/networking layer in front of it?' A successful port-forward shows the Pod works and is reachable directly, so a Service that still fails points at the selector/Endpoints/kube-proxy layer. The “The problem must be inside the Pod's…” option draws the opposite conclusion from the evidence. The “The comparison is meaningless, since port-forward…” option is a made-up constraint: port-forward maps an arbitrary local port to the Pod's container port, with no incompatibility with Service port numbers. The “The problem must be a liveness probe…” option narrows the cause to one probe type when the evidence points at the networking layer.

assessments.prompt: Walk through, in order, the full diagnostic sequence you'd use for a Pod reported as 'broken' with no other information given, explaining what question each command answers and why the order matters.
assessments.modelAnswer: The first command is always kubectl get pods, to read the STATUS and RESTARTS columns. It's the cheapest check and it narrows down which lifecycle stage is broken: never scheduled (Pending), image-pull failure (ImagePullBackOff), repeated crashing (CrashLoopBackOff, or a climbing RESTARTS count even while showing Running), or Running with an application-level problem that isn't visible at this level. The second command is kubectl describe pod, read for its Events section at the bottom. It answers 'at which stage, in which component, did things go wrong,' since each event Reason (FailedScheduling, Pulling/Pulled, Started, Unhealthy, BackOff) maps onto a part of the pipeline from the Cluster Architecture concept. This step comes before logs or exec because it can resolve the whole question if the Pod never got far enough to run application code: a scheduling failure or an image pull problem has nothing to do with the inside of the container, and reaching for logs or exec first would be looking in the wrong place. Only once describe confirms the container has started at least once do kubectl logs --previous (for a Pod that has crashed) or plain kubectl logs (for a Pod that's Running) become the right step, since the application's own stdout/stderr can explain a logic-level failure the platform-level tools can't see. Finally, if the container is Running and logs haven't solved it, kubectl exec lets you inspect live state (resolved environment variables, file contents under a mounted volume, connectivity to a dependency). It's the most expensive and invasive of the four tools, so it comes last, once the cheaper checks have shown that the problem is something exec can help answer.

concepts.title: Liveness vs. Readiness Probes
concepts.description: A liveness probe answers 'should this container be killed and restarted' while a readiness probe answers 'should this Pod currently receive traffic.' They are different questions with different consequences, and conflating them is one of the most common ways teams cause their own crash loops or route requests to Pods that can't handle them yet.
learningObjectives: Explain precisely what a liveness probe controls (kubelet-initiated container restart) versus what a readiness probe controls (Service Endpoints membership), and why conflating them causes real incidents.
Configure httpGet, exec, and tcpSocket probe types, and choose the right one for a given application.
Explain the role of initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, timeoutSeconds, and failureThreshold, and predict how misconfiguring them induces a crash loop under load.
Explain how a startupProbe interacts with a liveness probe for slow-starting applications, and why omitting one is a common cause of false-positive restarts.
Predict, for a given probe configuration and application behavior, whether a struggling Pod gets restarted, gets removed from Service traffic, or both.
Debug a Pod that's Running but receiving no traffic by inspecting its readiness probe configuration and its Service's Endpoints.

sections.heading: Two Different Questions, Two Different Consequences
sections.body:
A **liveness probe** answers one question, repeatedly, for the lifetime of a container: 'is this process stuck, deadlocked, or otherwise broken beyond its own ability to recover?' If it fails enough consecutive times, the kubelet's response is decisive: it kills the container and restarts it, as if the process had crashed on its own, incrementing the Pod's restart count.

A **readiness probe** answers a different question: 'is this container, right now, in a state where it should receive requests?' Its consequence is non-destructive. A failing readiness probe leaves the container running; it only removes the Pod from the Endpoints/EndpointSlice objects backing any Service that selects it (the mechanism from the Services concept), so traffic stops being routed there until readiness passes again.

This distinction matters most because the two failure modes look different and need different fixes. A container killed and restarted over and over is a liveness problem (or a genuine application crash). A container that's alive and stable, RESTARTS: 0, but whose Service has empty Endpoints is a readiness problem. Reaching for a liveness-shaped fix for a readiness-shaped symptom, or vice versa, wastes debugging time because you're solving the wrong mechanism.

sections.heading: Probe Types: httpGet, exec, tcpSocket
sections.body:
All three probe types can be used for either a livenessProbe or a readinessProbe; the checking mechanism is the same regardless of what you do with the result.

```yaml
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 10

readinessProbe:
  exec:
    command: ["cat", "/tmp/ready"]
  periodSeconds: 5

# A third type, for anything that isn't HTTP and doesn't need a custom script:
livenessProbe:
  tcpSocket:
    port: 5432
  periodSeconds: 10
```

`httpGet` issues an HTTP GET against the given path and port and treats any response from 200 to 399 as success. It fits anything that already exposes an HTTP server, since most frameworks make a dedicated `/healthz` or `/ready` endpoint cheap. `exec` runs a command *inside* the container and treats exit code 0 as success, which is useful when readiness depends on something an HTTP endpoint can't easily express (a file's existence, a small script checking several internal conditions). `tcpSocket` attempts to open a TCP connection to the given port and treats a successful connection as success, with no awareness of the application layer above it. It suits services that don't speak HTTP (a raw TCP protocol, a database), but it's also the weakest signal of the three, since a port accepting connections says nothing about whether the process behind it is working. (There is also a native `grpc` probe type for services that implement the gRPC health-checking protocol.) Failed probes of any type leave a `Warning Unhealthy` event in `kubectl describe pod`, which is the first place to confirm which probe is failing and with what message.

sections.heading: The Timing Knobs and the Classic Misconfiguration
sections.body:
Every probe shares the same timing fields: `initialDelaySeconds` (how long to wait after the container starts before the first check), `periodSeconds` (how often to repeat), `timeoutSeconds` (how long one check may take before counting as a failure), and `failureThreshold`/`successThreshold` (how many consecutive failures or successes flip the reported state; `successThreshold` must be 1 for liveness and startup probes).

Here's the classic bug: a liveness probe with `timeoutSeconds: 1` and `failureThreshold: 1`, pointed at an endpoint that's normally fast but occasionally takes 2-3 seconds under load (a GC pause, a spike in concurrent requests, a slow downstream call the health-check handler touches). Under load, exactly when the application is most likely busy rather than broken, the probe times out, the kubelet counts a liveness failure, and with `failureThreshold: 1` a single slow response gets the container killed and restarted. The application wasn't unresponsive; the probe's timing was too tight for a normal, transient slowdown. Restarting a healthy-but-slow container fixes nothing: it interrupts in-flight requests, and if the load persists, the new container may hit the same slow window shortly after starting, producing a self-inflicted crash loop whose root cause is the probe's configuration, not the application. The fix, once diagnosed, is a materially looser `timeoutSeconds` and a `failureThreshold` of at least 3, since liveness should fire only for a *sustained* failure to respond, not one slow tick.

sections.heading: startupProbe: Protecting Slow-Starting Apps From Their Own Liveness Probe
sections.body:
Before `startupProbe` existed, the workaround for an application with a long, variable startup (a JVM warming up, a large in-memory cache loading, migrations running) was a very large `initialDelaySeconds` on the liveness probe. That has a side effect: it also delays detecting a *truly* hung application well past its normal startup window, since liveness checks don't begin until the whole delay has elapsed.

```yaml
startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 10   # allows up to 300s (30 * 10s) for startup
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3  # tight and fast, but only once startupProbe has succeeded
```

`startupProbe` runs first, on its own schedule, and **disables** both the liveness and readiness probes until it succeeds once. After that it stops running, and liveness/readiness take over on their own schedules. This gets the best of both settings: a generous budget for the variable startup phase (`failureThreshold: 30` at `periodSeconds: 10` here permits up to 5 minutes), and a tight, fast liveness probe (`failureThreshold: 3` at `periodSeconds: 5`, about 15 seconds to detect a real hang) once the application has finished starting and later slowness is far more likely to be a real problem worth restarting for.

sections.heading: Readiness Misconfiguration: Traffic to Unready Pods, or Perpetually Excluded Pods
sections.body:
Readiness misconfiguration fails in two opposite directions, and both are common. The first is **no readiness probe at all**. Without one, a Pod counts as Ready as soon as its containers are Running, regardless of whether the application has finished warming up (loading a cache, opening a connection pool, registering with something else). A Service pointed at such a Pod routes real traffic to it the instant it's Running, even if the application would error or hang on that first request. This is the footgun from the Services concept, and the reason nearly every production workload should define an explicit readinessProbe instead of relying on the Running-implies-Ready default.

The second is a readiness probe that checks something **too strict, or unrelated to this Pod's own ability to serve traffic**. A common example pings a downstream dependency (a third-party API, a shared cache) that's occasionally flaky for reasons unrelated to this Pod's health. Every Pod of that Service then bounces in and out of Ready in near-lockstep whenever the dependency hiccups, cutting the Service's serving capacity for a problem a per-Pod check can't detect or fix: a shared dependency being down affects every Pod equally, so it says nothing about *this* Pod relative to its siblings. The guidance: readiness should check whether *this process* can currently do its job, its own internal state, not the transitive health of everything it talks to.

examples.title: Distinct Liveness and Readiness Endpoints on One Container
examples.code:
containers:
  - name: app
    image: my-app:1.4
    ports:
      - containerPort: 8080
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz     # "is the process itself alive and not deadlocked?"
        port: 8080
      periodSeconds: 10
      timeoutSeconds: 3
      failureThreshold: 3
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready        # "can I currently serve real requests?"
        port: 8080
      periodSeconds: 5
      timeoutSeconds: 2
      failureThreshold: 2
examples.explanation: Using two endpoints lets each probe check what it's meant to. /healthz might do almost nothing beyond confirming the process can respond, kept shallow so it stays fast and reliable and fails only for a genuinely stuck process, since failing it is destructive. /ready might check that the database connection pool is initialized and a startup cache warm-up has completed. It can be stricter because failing it only excludes the Pod from traffic, a much safer response to a marginal or uncertain state than restarting the container. Pointing both probes at the same endpoint with the same thresholds throws this distinction away and risks treating a readiness-shaped problem (temporarily can't serve requests) as a liveness-shaped one (kill and restart), a far more disruptive response than the situation calls for.

examples.title: A Liveness Probe Misconfiguration Inducing a Self-Caused Crash Loop
examples.code:
# livenessProbe: httpGet /healthz, timeoutSeconds: 1, periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 1

kubectl describe pod web-abc123 | tail -8
# Events:
#   Warning  Unhealthy  40s (x1 over 40s)  kubelet  Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.244.1.9:8080/healthz": context deadline exceeded
#   Normal   Killing    40s                kubelet  Container app failed liveness probe, will be restarted
#   Normal   Started    38s                kubelet  Started container app
#   Warning  Unhealthy  10s                kubelet  Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.244.1.9:8080/healthz": context deadline exceeded
#   Normal   Killing    10s                kubelet  Container app failed liveness probe, will be restarted
examples.explanation: With timeoutSeconds: 1 and failureThreshold: 1, one HTTP response slower than a second is enough to trigger a kill-and-restart, with no tolerance for even one transient slow tick. If the application is under load and its /healthz handler, even a cheap one, occasionally takes 1.2 seconds because of scheduling delay or a GC pause, this configuration restarts a working container because of the load, not because anything is broken. If the same load persists across the restart, the new container may hit the same timeout shortly after starting, producing the repeating pattern shown. The fix is loosening timeoutSeconds (to something like 3-5s) and raising failureThreshold to at least 3, so only a sustained, repeated failure to respond, not one slow tick, triggers a restart.

examples.title: startupProbe Giving a Slow-Starting App Room, Without Weakening Liveness Afterward
examples.code:
# WITHOUT startupProbe: liveness alone, forced to compromise
# livenessProbe: initialDelaySeconds: 120 (guesses the worst-case startup time),
#                periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 3
# A hang that happens early (say 30s in) isn't noticed until the fixed 120s delay
# has passed, then another ~15s of failed checks.

# WITH startupProbe: the two concerns are separated
# startupProbe:  failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 10   (up to 300s to start)
# livenessProbe: periodSeconds: 5,  failureThreshold: 3    (only ~15s to detect a hang, but ONLY once startupProbe has already succeeded once)

kubectl describe pod web-abc123 | grep 'Startup probe'
# Warning  Unhealthy  3m50s (x24 over 4m)  kubelet  Startup probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503
# (the failures stop once the startup probe first succeeds; a successful probe emits no event)
examples.explanation: Without a startupProbe, the fixed 120-second initialDelaySeconds must cover the worst startup time this application has shown, and it's a flat, unconditional wait applied on every start whether or not the app needed it. A hang during that window goes unnoticed, and even afterward the liveness probe needs its failure threshold to detect one. With a startupProbe, the startup phase gets its own generous, repeatedly checked budget (up to 300 seconds here, but ending the moment the app becomes healthy instead of waiting out a fixed timer), and liveness begins on its own tight schedule once startup has finished, so a real post-startup hang is caught in about 15 seconds regardless of how long the worst-case cold start takes. The describe output shows the startup probe failing, as expected, while the app warms up; once it first succeeds, no more failures appear and the other probes take over.

misconceptions.description: Liveness and readiness probes are essentially the same mechanism used at two different moments -- pointing both at the same endpoint with the same settings gives you full protection either way.
misconceptions.clarification: They have different consequences on failure: a failed liveness probe destroys and restarts the container; a failed readiness probe excludes the Pod from Service traffic and leaves it running. Because the consequences differ so much, what each probe should check often differs too. Liveness should verify something narrow like 'is the process responsive at all,' since failing it is destructive and should happen only for a stuck process, while readiness can check stricter, more application-specific conditions (a warm cache, an open DB pool), since failing it only pauses traffic. Pointing a liveness probe at a check suited to readiness (like a downstream dependency ping) risks restarting a healthy container over a problem a restart can't fix.

misconceptions.description: A container that fails its liveness probe gets restarted, but it stays counted as a normal Service backend the whole time, since only readiness failures affect traffic routing.
misconceptions.clarification: A liveness failure does affect traffic, indirectly: once the kubelet kills the container, the Pod's containers are no longer all running, so the Pod is no longer Ready and drops out of the Service's Endpoints for the duration of the restart. A killed container can't be ready to serve anything. What matters is which mechanism is doing the excluding: a readiness failure alone (container still Running, just reported not-ready) removes a Pod from traffic non-destructively and reversibly once readiness passes again, while a liveness failure removes it only as a side effect of the more disruptive act of killing and restarting the container.

exercises.prompt: A Deployment's Pod template defines a livenessProbe but no readinessProbe at all. The application takes about 20 seconds after the container starts to finish connecting to its database, and would error on any request received before that. What happens to traffic sent to this Pod via its Service in the first 20 seconds after the container reaches the Running state?
exercises.code:
containers:
  - name: app
    image: my-app:1.0
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
    # no readinessProbe defined
hints: With no readinessProbe at all, what does a Pod's Ready condition default to, based purely on its containers' Running state?
Endpoints/EndpointSlice membership is driven by the Ready condition -- not by whether a readinessProbe exists, and not by anything the liveness probe is checking.
The 20-second database connection window is invisible to Kubernetes entirely if nothing is explicitly checking for it.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The Pod is considered Ready as soon as its container is Running (the default with no readinessProbe), so the Service adds it to Endpoints and starts routing real traffic to it immediately -- including during the 20-second window before its database connection is actually ready, during which any request it receives will error.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Without a readinessProbe, Kubernetes has no way to know that this application needs about 20 seconds after starting before it can handle requests. The only probe is liveness, which starts after initialDelaySeconds: 5 and checks something else (process responsiveness), not 'is the DB connection ready.' With no readiness signal, the Pod's Ready condition becomes true as soon as its container is Running, so it's added to the Service's Endpoints immediately and receives traffic well before the 20-second warm-up finishes, producing request errors. The fix is a readinessProbe (for example an httpGet against a /ready endpoint that the app reports healthy only once its DB connection is established) so the Pod is excluded from traffic during that window.

exercises.prompt: This Deployment's Pods keep entering CrashLoopBackOff under moderate load, even though application-level logs (from kubectl logs --previous) show no errors or crashes at all -- just normal request handling right up until the container is killed. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 1
  failureThreshold: 1
hints: If the application's own logs show no crash or error at all, the thing actually killing the container might not be the application's own code.
timeoutSeconds: 1 combined with failureThreshold: 1 means exactly how much tolerance for a single slow response, under any amount of load?
The fix should loosen the probe's own tolerance for transient slowness, not change anything about the application.
exercises.solutionCode:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 3
  failureThreshold: 3
exercises.solutionExplanation: Clean application logs with no crash, paired with restarts that line up with Killing/Unhealthy events in kubectl describe pod, point at the liveness probe as the thing killing healthy containers. With timeoutSeconds: 1 and failureThreshold: 1, a single HTTP response taking just over a second, the kind of transient slowdown moderate load easily causes, counts as a liveness failure and triggers an immediate kill-and-restart. Raising timeoutSeconds to 3 gives each check more headroom before it counts as failed, and raising failureThreshold to 3 requires three consecutive failures (about 15 seconds of sustained unresponsiveness at periodSeconds: 5) before a restart, instead of one isolated slow tick. That turns the probe from something that reacts to normal load variance into something that reacts only to a sustained hang, which is what liveness should check.

assessments.prompt: A Pod's readiness probe starts failing repeatedly while its liveness probe continues to pass. What happens to this Pod?
options: The kubelet restarts the container, since any failing probe eventually triggers a restart.
The Pod is deleted entirely and a replacement is scheduled by its controller.
The container keeps running untouched, but the Pod is removed from any Service's Endpoints until readiness starts passing again.
Nothing happens at all -- only liveness probe results have any observable effect on the cluster, and readiness is used purely for display in kubectl.
assessments.explanation: A failing readiness probe never triggers a restart or deletion on its own; its effect is on Service routing: the Pod is excluded from the relevant Endpoints/EndpointSlice objects, so traffic stops being sent to it, while the container keeps running and can receive traffic again as soon as readiness passes. The “The kubelet restarts the container, since any…” option conflates the two probe types' consequences; only a failing liveness probe causes a restart. The “The Pod is deleted entirely…” option describes something no probe does by itself (that's a controller concern). The “Nothing happens at all -- only liveness…” option is the misconception this concept corrects: a failing readiness probe has an observable effect, a non-destructive, traffic-routing one.

assessments.prompt: A team configures a livenessProbe with `tcpSocket: { port: 5432 }` for a Postgres container. The process inside has deadlocked internally -- it still accepts new TCP connections but never actually responds to any query -- yet the liveness probe keeps reporting success indefinitely. Why?
options: tcpSocket probes are broken by design and never actually execute; the container would need an httpGet or exec probe to have any liveness protection at all.
tcpSocket only verifies that a TCP connection can be opened to the given port -- it has no awareness of anything at the application layer above that.
tcpSocket probes only run once, at container startup, and never repeat -- so a deadlock occurring after that first successful check would never be detected by design.
tcpSocket probes require a correspondingly-configured readinessProbe of the same type before they will ever report a failure.
assessments.explanation: tcpSocket only attempts to open a TCP connection, with no awareness of the application layer above it, which makes it the weakest of the three probe types: a port accepting connections says nothing about whether the process behind it is working. A deadlocked-but-still-listening process is the blind spot this probe type has by design. The “tcpSocket probes are broken by design…” option is false: tcpSocket probes run and check something real, just something narrow. The “tcpSocket probes only run once, at container…” option is false; probes repeat every periodSeconds. The “tcpSocket probes require a correspondingly-configured readinessProbe…” option invents a dependency between probe types; a livenessProbe works independently of any readinessProbe.

assessments.prompt: A Pod defines both a startupProbe and a livenessProbe. During the first 60 seconds after the container starts, while the application is still warming up, what is the livenessProbe actually doing?
options: It runs at a permanently slower periodSeconds during this window, automatically multiplied by whatever failureThreshold the startupProbe itself uses.
It runs, but any failures during this window are silently discarded and never counted toward failureThreshold; only once the startupProbe succeeds do failures start counting.
It's running on its own normal schedule the entire time, exactly as if no startupProbe were configured, and could restart the container if it happens to fail during warm-up.

It is not running at all yet -- startupProbe specifically disables both the liveness and readiness probes until it succeeds at least once; only after that does the livenessProbe begin executing on its own configured schedule.
assessments.explanation: startupProbe runs first, on its own schedule, and disables the liveness and readiness probes until it succeeds once; after that it stops, and liveness/readiness run on their own schedules. So the livenessProbe isn't executing during this window, rather than just having its failures ignored. The “It's running on its own normal schedule…” option ignores the purpose of startupProbe, which is to keep liveness from acting during startup. The “It runs, but any failures during…” option invents a run-but-discard behavior. The “It runs at a permanently slower periodSeconds…” option invents a schedule-multiplication effect that doesn't exist.

assessments.prompt: A Service has 5 Pods, and each one's readinessProbe checks connectivity to a shared third-party API. That third-party API becomes briefly flaky. What happens, and why is this considered a readiness-probe design mistake per this concept?
options: All 5 Pods tend to bounce out of Ready in near-lockstep, needlessly cutting the Service's entire serving capacity -- because a shared dependency being down affects every Pod equally, it isn't information about any individual Pod's own health relative to its siblings, which is exactly what a per-Pod readiness check is supposed to measure.
Only the one Pod that happens to check the API during the flaky window drops out of Endpoints; the other 4 continue serving traffic normally, completely unaffected.
Nothing happens, since readiness probes are only capable of checking conditions local to the Pod's own container filesystem, never anything reachable over the network.
This is actually the correct, recommended design -- readiness probes should always check every downstream dependency a Pod talks to, regardless of how shared or external it is.
assessments.explanation: Checking a shared dependency in a readiness probe means every Pod of that Service bounces in and out of Ready in near-lockstep whenever the dependency hiccups, cutting the Service's serving capacity for a problem a per-Pod check can't detect or fix. Readiness should check whether this specific process is currently able to do its job, not the transitive health of everything it talks to. The “Only the one Pod that happens…” option wrongly assumes independence across Pods that a shared-dependency check doesn't provide. The “This is actually the correct, recommended design…” option contradicts this concept's guidance. The “Nothing happens, since readiness probes are only…” option is false: exec and httpGet readiness checks routinely reach over the network; nothing restricts them to the local filesystem.

assessments.prompt: A team's Pods are crash-looping under moderate production load, but the application's own logs show no errors. They suspect the liveness probe. Explain, mechanistically, how a liveness probe misconfiguration alone can produce exactly this symptom, and what specifically about the probe's configuration needs to change.
assessments.modelAnswer: A liveness probe answers 'should this container be killed and restarted,' and it decides purely from its configured timing: timeoutSeconds (how long one check may take before it counts as failed) and failureThreshold (how many consecutive failures the kubelet requires before it acts). If those are too tight for the application's healthy response-time variance under real load (for example timeoutSeconds: 1 with failureThreshold: 1), then a single health check that takes 1.2 seconds because the process is busy with a burst of requests (a GC pause, scheduling contention, a slow downstream call inside the health-check handler) is treated the same as a hung process: the kubelet kills and restarts the container. That explains the symptom: the application's logs show no error because there was no application bug; the process was doing its job, slightly slower than the probe's timeout allowed, and the platform decided to kill it. Under continued load the restarted container can hit the same slow window again, producing a repeating crash loop whose root cause is the probe's timing, not the application. The fix is to loosen both dimensions of tolerance: raise timeoutSeconds enough to cover the application's normal (not just best-case) response time under load, and raise failureThreshold to require several consecutive failures before treating the situation as a hang worth a restart. The principle is that a liveness probe should fire only for sustained unresponsiveness, since killing the container is destructive and should be reserved for situations a restart can fix, which a single slow tick under normal load isn't.

assessments.prompt: After a deploy, pods keep restarting in a loop and the service is down, although the app works fine locally. The liveness probe hits /health with a 1-second timeout and starts after 5 seconds. How do you troubleshoot and fix this?
assessments.modelAnswer: Check kubectl describe pod for events showing 'Liveness probe failed' and kubectl logs --previous to see what the app was doing before it was killed. A common cause is a slow start: the JVM or migrations take 30 seconds, so the liveness probe fails after 5 seconds and the kubelet restarts the container before it is ready, forever. Another is a /health endpoint that checks the database, so a slow dependency makes Kubernetes kill healthy pods. Fix by adding a startupProbe with a generous failure threshold so liveness only begins once the app has started, increasing timeouts, and making liveness a cheap 'process is alive' check. Use a readiness probe for dependency checks, which removes the pod from Service endpoints without restarting it. Finally make sure resource limits are not causing OOM kills that look similar.

concepts.title: Resource Requests and Limits
concepts.description: requests and limits look like a matched pair but are enforced by different mechanisms at different times: requests steer the scheduler's placement decision, while limits are enforced by the kernel at runtime. Understanding why a memory limit violation gets a container killed (OOMKilled) while a CPU limit violation only gets it throttled is the key to telling 'my Pod died' from 'my Pod is just slow.'
learningObjectives: Distinguish what requests are used for (scheduling placement) from what limits are used for (runtime enforcement).
Explain precisely why exceeding a memory limit gets a container OOMKilled, while exceeding a CPU limit only throttles it, tracing the difference to compressible versus incompressible resources.
Describe the three QoS classes (Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort), how each is derived automatically from a Pod's requests/limits, and their consequence for node-pressure eviction order.
Read kubectl describe pod output to distinguish an OOMKilled Pod from a CPU-throttled-but-otherwise-healthy Pod.
Explain the purpose of a namespace-level LimitRange and the risk it mitigates when a Pod spec omits resources entirely.
Predict the practical consequence, across many Pods on a node, of setting limits far above requests (overcommit) versus setting requests equal to limits everywhere.

sections.heading: Requests: What the Scheduler Uses
sections.body:
`resources.requests` is the claim the scheduler uses when deciding which node a Pod can go on. CPU is written in cores or millicores (`1` equals `1000m`), and memory in bytes with suffixes such as `Mi` and `Gi` (note that `M` and `Mi` differ: 1M is 1,000,000 bytes, 1Mi is 1,048,576). The scheduler sums the requests of every Pod already assigned to a node and considers that node valid only if enough *unallocated* capacity remains (measured against the node's allocatable resources, which are less than its raw capacity because the system and kubelet reserve some) to cover the new Pod's requests too. That is the mechanism behind the `0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu` failure from the Cluster Architecture concept. Requests are not checked against actual usage once the Pod is scheduled, but they still matter at runtime in two ways: the CPU request sets the container's relative CPU weight when the node is contended, and requests feed the Pod's QoS class and so the eviction order described below.

A container with **no `requests` and no `limits`** is treated as requesting nothing from the scheduler's point of view. That sounds harmless but is a real risk: the scheduler will stack such a Pod onto a node assuming it needs zero reserved capacity, even if it goes on to use a lot of CPU or memory. Enough unrequested Pods on one node is how a node ends up overcommitted, with more real usage than capacity, even though every scheduling decision looked fine on paper. (If a container sets limits but omits requests, Kubernetes defaults each missing request to the limit value.)

sections.heading: Limits: Enforced at Runtime by the Kernel, Not the Scheduler
sections.body:
`resources.limits` has nothing to do with the scheduler. When the kubelet starts a container, it configures the node's cgroup (control group) settings for that container's process according to its `limits`: a local, per-node, per-container mechanism, enforced continuously by the kernel for as long as the container runs, independent of what the scheduler decided earlier.

That corrects a natural but wrong assumption: the API server doesn't check limits on an ongoing basis, and no component other than the kubelet and container runtime on that one node is involved. A Pod can be scheduled successfully (a `requests`-driven decision, made once, by the scheduler, and visible afterward under `Allocated resources` in `kubectl describe node`) and then have its containers throttled or killed repeatedly (a `limits`-driven outcome, enforced continuously, by the kernel). These are two separate mechanisms operating at two separate times.

sections.heading: Why Memory Limits Kill and CPU Limits Throttle
sections.body:
This is the most commonly confused fact in this topic, and it comes down to one property: **memory is incompressible; CPU time is compressible.**

Memory can't be 'slowed down': a process has the RAM it's holding or it doesn't, and the kernel can't make a process use less without freeing something, which it can't decide on the application's behalf. So when a container's memory usage hits its cgroup limit and the process tries to allocate more, the kernel's OOM killer terminates the process with `SIGKILL`. `kubectl describe pod` shows `Last State: Terminated`, `Reason: OOMKilled`, `Exit Code: 137` (the Unix convention of 128 + signal number; SIGKILL is signal 9, so 128 + 9 = 137). This is a hard, immediate stop, with no warning period and no gradual degradation. Runtimes with their own memory management need to be told about the limit: a JVM sized by its own defaults, for example, can try to grow its heap past the container's limit, so flags such as `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` exist to keep the heap inside it.

CPU is about *time slices*, and time slices can be withheld without killing anything. The kernel's CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) bandwidth controller, which enforces CPU limits, tracks how much CPU time a container's cgroup has used within each accounting period (typically 100ms), and once the quota for the current period is used up, the container's processes aren't scheduled for more CPU time until the next period begins. They keep existing, keep their memory and state, and run slower, in short, repeated pauses. Kubernetes calls this **throttling**, and a throttled container never shows as `OOMKilled`, never restarts because of it, and its RESTARTS count doesn't move from CPU throttling alone. It takes longer to do everything, often without any obvious sign at a quick glance.

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 500m      # exceeding this: throttled, not killed
    memory: 512Mi   # exceeding this: OOMKilled (SIGKILL, exit 137)
```

sections.heading: QoS Classes: Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort
sections.body:
Kubernetes derives a **Quality of Service (QoS) class** for every Pod from the shape of its containers' requests and limits. There's no field to set; it's computed.

**Guaranteed**: every container in the Pod has CPU and memory `requests` equal to `limits`. **Burstable**: at least one container has a request or limit set, but the Pod doesn't meet the Guaranteed condition (the common, realistic middle case: some slack between what's reserved and what's allowed). **BestEffort**: no container in the Pod sets any requests or limits.

The class matters during **node-pressure eviction**: when a node is low on a resource (commonly memory) and the kubelet must reclaim some by evicting whole Pods, it favors evicting `BestEffort` Pods first (they reserved nothing, so they're least entitled to the node's capacity), then `Burstable` Pods (roughly in order of how far over their requests they're running, so the ones using the most unreserved slack go first), and `Guaranteed` Pods last, only in extreme circumstances, since their usage was never supposed to exceed what was reserved. (The kubelet's actual ranking also considers whether usage exceeds requests and Pod priority, but this order is the useful rule of thumb.) For latency-sensitive or critical workloads, `Guaranteed` is generally the right choice, trading some flexibility for the strongest protection against being evicted first under node pressure.

sections.heading: LimitRange and the Cost of Forgetting Limits Entirely
sections.body:
A `LimitRange` object, applied to a namespace, lets a cluster operator set default `requests`/`limits` for any container that doesn't specify its own, plus min/max bounds on what any container in that namespace may declare:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 512Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      max:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 2Gi
```

Without something like this, a container spec that forgets to declare `resources` doesn't fail or get rejected; it becomes `BestEffort`, with zero reserved capacity from the scheduler's point of view and no ceiling on the CPU or memory it can use at runtime. That's a textbook 'noisy neighbor' setup: one forgotten `resources` block can let a container consume unbounded memory on a node until it starves every other Pod there. A `LimitRange` closes that gap with a sane default for every container in the namespace even when its author forgot to think about resources, a safety net for a mistake that's otherwise invisible until it causes an incident. Separately, setting `limits` far above `requests` cluster-wide (deliberate overcommit, betting that not every Pod needs its full limit at once, for better average node utilization) versus setting `requests` equal to `limits` everywhere (fully reserved, `Guaranteed`, more predictable, lower density) is a capacity-planning tradeoff, with no single right answer.

examples.title: OOMKilled: Reading the Evidence in kubectl describe pod
examples.code:
kubectl describe pod web-abc123 | grep -A8 'Last State'
# Last State:     Terminated
#   Reason:       OOMKilled
#   Exit Code:    137
#   Started:      Wed, 12 Aug 2026 14:02:11 +0000
#   Finished:     Wed, 12 Aug 2026 14:04:47 +0000

kubectl get pod web-abc123
# NAME        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# web-abc123  1/1     Running   3          6m
examples.explanation: Exit Code: 137 with Reason: OOMKilled is the signature of a memory limit violation (exit 137 alone only says the process received SIGKILL, which also happens for other reasons, so the OOMKilled reason is what confirms memory): 137 decodes as 128 + 9 (SIGKILL), and OOMKilled identifies the kernel's OOM killer as the sender, triggered because this container's cgroup hit its memory limit and the kernel had no way to reclaim memory from it except terminating the process. RESTARTS: 3 shows the kubelet has already restarted this container several times; each restart gives it a fresh chance, and if the memory pattern (a leak, or a limit set below genuine peak usage) repeats, it will hit the same ceiling and get OOMKilled again, a slow-motion crash loop caused by memory pressure rather than an application bug or a probe misconfiguration.

examples.title: CPU Throttling: Slow, Not Dead, and Invisible to RESTARTS
examples.code:
kubectl get pod web-abc123
# NAME        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# web-abc123  1/1     Running   0          2h
# (Running, zero restarts, looks healthy from this view alone)

kubectl top pod web-abc123
# NAME        CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
# web-abc123  500m         310Mi
# (pinned at its cpu limit, 500m, for sustained periods, despite requests: 100m)

# Application-level symptom: request latency has crept up 4x under moderate load,
# with no errors and no crashes anywhere in kubectl logs.
examples.explanation: Nothing in kubectl get pod or RESTARTS suggests a problem, which is the trap with CPU throttling: it never kills anything, so none of the signals people check for 'is my Pod broken' (Running status, restart count, describe's Terminated/Reason fields) show anything unusual. kubectl top pod (which needs metrics-server installed) showing CPU pinned at the configured limit (500m), together with latency degradation and zero errors, is the signature of throttling: the kernel's CFS bandwidth controller denies the container more CPU time once it exhausts its quota for each period, so everything takes longer, with no crash, no restart, and no error in the logs, because nothing about the process is malfunctioning.

examples.title: A LimitRange Filling In for a Forgotten resources Block
examples.code:
# Namespace has this LimitRange already applied:
# defaultRequest: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
# default:        { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }

# A developer submits this Pod spec with NO resources block at all:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: forgot-resources
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0

# What actually gets scheduled and run (after the LimitRange's defaults are applied):
# containers:
#   - name: app
#     resources:
#       requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
#       limits:   { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }
examples.explanation: The developer's spec declares nothing under resources. In a namespace with no LimitRange this container would be BestEffort: no reservation for the scheduler and no ceiling at runtime. Because this namespace has a LimitRange with defaultRequest and default values, the API server's admission process fills them in at creation time, before the object is persisted, and the container ends up Burstable (requests set, but not equal to limits) with a 100m/128Mi reservation and a 500m/512Mi ceiling, without the developer thinking about resource sizing. That's the safety net this concept describes: a namespace-wide default that stops one forgotten resources block from becoming an unconstrained, unreserved container sharing a node with everything else.

misconceptions.description: Exceeding a CPU limit kills the container, the same way exceeding a memory limit does -- both are just "the resource ran out" in the same sense.
misconceptions.clarification: Only memory limit violations get the container killed (OOMKilled, exit code 137), because memory is incompressible: you can't make a process use less RAM instantly without terminating something. CPU time is compressible: the kernel's CFS bandwidth controller withholds additional CPU time from a container that has exhausted its quota for the current period, slowing it down (throttling) without touching its process. A CPU-limited container's RESTARTS count and Terminated/Reason fields are unaffected by throttling; the visible symptom is degraded performance, checked with something like kubectl top or latency metrics, not the Pod's lifecycle status.

misconceptions.description: If a container sets no resources at all, Kubernetes still gives it a sensible default request automatically, so the scheduler always reserves something for every container.
misconceptions.clarification: Without a LimitRange, a container that sets nothing gets no requests: the scheduler treats it as needing no reserved capacity (and it becomes BestEffort), however much it uses at runtime. Kubernetes does copy limits into requests when a container sets limits but omits requests, but that applies only when limits are present. Defaults for a container with no resources block come only from something explicit like a namespace LimitRange with a defaultRequest, applied by the API server at admission time. A BestEffort container can therefore be scheduled onto a node with no regard for whether it has capacity, which is the overcommit risk this concept describes.

exercises.prompt: A container has `requests: { memory: 128Mi }` and `limits: { memory: 256Mi }`. At runtime, its process tries to allocate memory until it's using 300Mi. What specifically happens, and what would `kubectl describe pod` show afterward?
hints: requests only affected the scheduler's placement decision, made once, before this container ever started running -- it plays no role in what happens now.
300Mi exceeds the LIMIT (256Mi), not just the request. Memory is incompressible -- what does the kernel do when a cgroup's memory limit is exceeded?
Think about the specific Reason and Exit Code kubectl describe pod reports for exactly this kind of termination.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The container is killed by the kernel's OOM killer the moment its actual usage tries to exceed the 256Mi limit. The 128Mi request is irrelevant at this point; it only mattered for scheduling. kubectl describe pod would show Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137, and the kubelet would then restart the container per its restartPolicy, incrementing RESTARTS.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The 128Mi request mattered at scheduling time; it plays no role in what happens when the container allocates past its limit. What matters now is the 256Mi limit, enforced continuously by the kernel via the container's cgroup: memory is incompressible, so the kernel can't make the process use less RAM when it allocates past the limit. Instead the OOM killer sends SIGKILL and terminates the process. kubectl describe pod reports Reason: OOMKilled with Exit Code: 137 (128 + signal 9), and, depending on the Pod's restartPolicy (Always, by default, for Pods managed by a Deployment), the kubelet restarts the container, which makes RESTARTS climb. If the process's memory needs exceed 256Mi under normal operation rather than as a one-off spike, the OOMKilled cycle will repeat until the limit is raised or the application's memory usage is reduced.

exercises.prompt: A team reports their application has become mysteriously slow under load -- 4x higher latency than before -- but there are no errors in the logs, RESTARTS is 0, and the Pod has been continuously Running for hours with no crashes at all. Given this resources block, identify the likely cause and fix it.
exercises.code:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 512Mi
hints: No crashes and no restarts rules out OOMKilled entirely -- that leaves the OTHER resource dimension as the likely suspect.

cpu requests and cpu limits are set to the exact same value here (100m) -- what does that mean for how much CPU time this container is ever allowed to use, even briefly, even if the node has plenty of idle CPU sitting unused?
100m is a small fraction of a single core (0.1 CPU). Compare that against what a moderately loaded application would realistically need.
exercises.solutionCode:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 1000m
    memory: 512Mi
exercises.solutionExplanation: With the CPU limit at 100m (a tenth of a core) and no crashes or restarts, this is a CPU throttling symptom, not a memory or crash one: the kernel's CFS bandwidth controller denies the container additional CPU time every time it exhausts its small per-period quota, which shows up purely as slowness, here the 4x latency increase, with no trace in RESTARTS, Terminated reasons, or logs, because nothing about the process is failing. Raising the cpu limit to 1000m (a full core) gives the container headroom under load before it's throttled again, and raising the cpu request to 500m makes the scheduler reserve enough CPU on whichever node this Pod lands on to make that higher limit usable in practice, instead of relying on unreserved, possibly contended capacity.

assessments.prompt: A Pod has one container with `requests: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }` and `limits: { cpu: 400m, memory: 256Mi }`. What QoS class does this Pod get, and why?
options: Guaranteed, because memory requests equal memory limits.
This is an invalid configuration and the Pod will be rejected by the API server.
BestEffort, because at least one resource type (cpu) has a gap between requests and limits, and any such gap drops it to the lowest class.
Burstable, because cpu requests (200m) do not equal cpu limits (400m), even though memory requests equal memory limits.
assessments.explanation: Guaranteed requires requests to equal limits for BOTH cpu AND memory in every container of the Pod. Here memory matches (256Mi == 256Mi) but cpu doesn't (200m requested vs. 400m limit), so the Pod isn't Guaranteed. It has requests set (ruling out BestEffort, which requires no requests or limits at all), so it's Burstable. The “Guaranteed, because memory requests equal memory limits” option wrongly treats matching on one resource as enough. The “BestEffort, because at least one resource type…” option misapplies BestEffort, which means no requests or limits are declared at all, not merely an unequal pair. The “This is an invalid configuration…” option is wrong: requests below limits for one resource and equal for another is valid and common (Burstable).

assessments.prompt: A container was scheduled with `requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }`. An hour after the Pod starts running successfully, does the kubelet or any other component continue checking this container's actual usage against its requests value on an ongoing basis?
options: No -- nothing checks actual usage against requests after scheduling; requests only fed the placement decision (and set relative CPU weight under contention). Only limits are enforced as ceilings, continuously, by the kernel.
Yes -- the API server polls every container's actual usage against its requests every few seconds and reschedules the Pod onto a different node if usage no longer matches.
Yes, but only for Guaranteed QoS class Pods -- Burstable and BestEffort Pods have their requests value ignored after scheduling as well as before.
Yes -- if actual usage ever drops below the requested value, the container is throttled to prevent it from using less than its own reservation.
assessments.explanation: Nothing re-checks a container's actual usage against its requests once it's running: requests were an input to the scheduler's placement decision (they also set the container's relative CPU weight under contention and feed its QoS class), but they are not enforced as a ceiling or floor. Limits are what the kernel enforces continuously via cgroups. The “Yes -- if actual usage ever drops…” option invents throttling for under-usage; throttling applies only to exceeding a limit, never to using less than a request. The “Yes -- the API server polls every…” option invents API-server polling and automatic rescheduling that Kubernetes doesn't have (Pods aren't silently moved between nodes after scheduling). The “Yes, but only for Guaranteed QoS class…” option invents a QoS-dependent exception that doesn't exist.

assessments.prompt: A container's spec sets `limits: { memory: 1Gi }` but no `requests` at all, in a namespace with no LimitRange configured. From the scheduler's point of view, how much memory does this container reserve when deciding where to place its Pod?
options: The Pod is rejected at admission time, since setting limits without a corresponding requests value is invalid.
1Gi, because when a container sets limits but omits requests, Kubernetes defaults the request to the limit value, so the scheduler reserves the full amount.
Effectively zero -- with no requests set and no LimitRange to supply a default, the scheduler treats the container as needing no reserved capacity, even though it can use up to 1Gi once running.
512Mi, exactly half of the limits value, as Kubernetes' built-in fallback ratio for any container missing an explicit request.
assessments.explanation: When a container sets limits but no requests, Kubernetes defaults each missing request to the limit value (if no LimitRange or other admission default applies first), so a memory limit of 1Gi becomes a memory request of 1Gi and the scheduler reserves the full amount. The “Effectively zero -- with no requests set…” option describes the case where neither requests nor limits are set, not this one. The “512Mi, exactly half of the limits value…” option invents a fallback ratio that Kubernetes doesn't have. The “The Pod is rejected at admission time…” option is false: a container may set limits without requests, and it isn't rejected.
