assessments.prompt: A namespace has a LimitRange with `defaultRequest: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }`. A developer applies a Pod spec whose container declares no `resources` block at all. What actually happens to that container's resources at creation time, and which component is responsible?
options: The scheduler consults the LimitRange only as a last resort, if the Pod would otherwise fail to schedule anywhere at all.
Nothing is filled in automatically; the LimitRange only produces a warning event, and the container still runs as BestEffort exactly as if no LimitRange existed.

The API server's admission process fills in the LimitRange's defaultRequest (and default limit, if configured) onto the container's spec at creation time, before the object is even persisted -- so the container ends up with a real, non-zero reservation without the developer having declared one explicitly.
The kubelet, on whichever node the Pod eventually lands on, retroactively edits the running container's cgroup settings to match the LimitRange sometime after scheduling has already happened.
assessments.explanation: The API server's admission process fills in the LimitRange defaults at creation time, before the object is persisted, so the container ends up Burstable with the LimitRange's defaults, and the developer never had to specify resources. The “Nothing is filled in automatically; the LimitRange…” option is wrong: the defaults are applied, not just warned about. The “The kubelet, on whichever node the Pod…” option misattributes the mechanism to the kubelet after scheduling, when it happens at admission time, before the Pod is scheduled. The “The scheduler consults the LimitRange only…” option invents a last-resort trigger; the LimitRange applies to any container missing its own values, whether or not scheduling would otherwise succeed.

assessments.prompt: Explain, mechanistically, why exceeding a memory limit results in a container being killed while exceeding a CPU limit only results in the container being throttled, tracing the explanation down to the actual kernel-level behavior involved.
assessments.modelAnswer: The core distinction is whether the resource is compressible or incompressible. Memory is incompressible: at any moment a process holds a certain amount of RAM or it doesn't, and the kernel can't make it use less without freeing something, which it can't safely do on the application's behalf since it doesn't know which allocations are safe to discard. So when a container's cgroup memory usage reaches its limit and the process tries to allocate more, the kernel's OOM killer terminates the process with SIGKILL. There's no intermediate state where the process is merely 'slowed down' with respect to memory, only an on/off boundary that ends in termination when crossed. Kubernetes reports this as Reason: OOMKilled with Exit Code: 137 (128 plus signal number 9, SIGKILL). CPU is compressible: it's a measure of processing time over an interval, and a process can be given less of it without being terminated; it runs more slowly. CPU limits are enforced by the kernel's CFS bandwidth controller, which tracks how much CPU time a container's cgroup has consumed within each short accounting period (commonly 100ms) and, once the quota is used up, declines to schedule that cgroup's processes until the next period begins. The process's memory, file descriptors, network connections, and other state are untouched; it just pauses repeatedly, which Kubernetes calls throttling. That's why the two failure modes look so different: an OOMKilled container shows a Terminated/Reason/Exit Code signature and a climbing RESTARTS count, while a CPU-throttled container shows none of that: Running, RESTARTS: 0, no log errors, and only degraded performance, detectable by measuring CPU usage (pinned at the limit) or latency, not from the Pod's basic status fields.

assessments.prompt: Your cluster nodes show plenty of free CPU on dashboards, yet new pods are stuck in Pending and some running pods are being OOMKilled. Explain what is going on and how you would fix it.
assessments.modelAnswer: The scheduler places pods based on requests, not actual usage. If teams set large CPU and memory requests that their apps never use, nodes look idle on usage graphs but are fully reserved, so new pods cannot fit and stay Pending (kubectl describe pod shows 'Insufficient cpu' or memory). Meanwhile pods whose memory limit is below their real peak get OOMKilled when they exceed it, since memory, unlike CPU, cannot be throttled. Fix by measuring real usage (metrics-server, Prometheus, or a VPA in recommendation mode), then setting requests close to typical usage and memory limits above the observed peak with headroom. Be careful with tight CPU limits, which cause throttling and latency. Add LimitRanges and ResourceQuotas for sensible defaults per namespace, and use the cluster autoscaler so genuine growth adds nodes.
